analysis.one_liner: Gives airline workers hiring priority and seniority protections when their routes are sold to another carrier.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by senators from both parties, got one subcommittee hearing but never a committee vote before Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: When one airline buys or takes over another airline's routes, this bill would have required the buyer to hire the seller's employees — by seniority, enough to run the route — and to honor their seniority standing. It also would have extended, from 10 to 17 years, the right of furloughed airline workers to be hired first when other airlines add staff. Workers could enforce these rights in federal court, with legal fees paid by the airline if they won.
analysis.who_benefits: Airline employees whose jobs are displaced by a route transfer: pilots, flight attendants, mechanics, and other staff of the carrier losing the routes, who would get guaranteed hiring by the new operator with their seniority honored. Furloughed airline workers of any age would gain a longer window (17 years instead of 10) during which hiring airlines must give them first consideration in their job specialty.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Airline workers displaced by route transfers

how_it_helps.text: When a route certificate is transferred, the acquiring airline must hire — in order of seniority — at least the number of employees the Transportation Secretary determines are needed to operate the route. [S2] [S3]

Those hired employees receive the seniority integration protections set out in the Tiger International Seaboard case, and can enforce them in U.S. district court, with attorneys' fees awarded against the airline if the worker substantially prevails. [S2] [S3]

The bill amends the Airline Deregulation Act of 1978 so employees furloughed or laid off without cause have a first right of hire — regardless of age — for 17 years after enactment, up from the current 10. [S2] [S3]
The protections would apply to any certificate transfer application filed on or after the date of introduction, July 26, 1991. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Airlines that acquire routes or hire additional employees would bear the costs: mandatory hiring from the transferring carrier's seniority list, integration of those employees' seniority, and potential court judgments and legal fees when workers sue to enforce the protections.
analysis.who_pays_short: Airlines acquiring routes or hiring staff

drawbacks.text: A mandatory duty to hire from the transferring carrier's seniority list constrains the acquiring airline's ability to choose its own workforce, which airlines could argue raises operating costs and limits flexibility — costs that could ultimately be reflected in fares. [S2] [S3]

Extending the furlough-hire priority from 10 to 17 years, and making it apply regardless of age, imposes a long-standing hiring preference on airlines that could make it harder for them to hire newer or younger candidates in a given specialty. [S2] [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the airline employees directly affected, the bill offered substantial, enforceable protection: a job with the buyer of their routes and legal recourse with paid fees. The costs fall on airlines in the form of hiring mandates and litigation exposure, which supporters would argue are modest compared with the disruption employees face when a carrier's routes are sold out from under them. The bill was never amended or debated on the floor, so no practical test of the trade-offs ever occurred.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, whose Aviation Subcommittee held one hearing in April 1992, but the committee never reported the bill and it never came to a vote before Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Sen. Bob Graham introduced the bill on July 26, 1991, for himself and Sen. Al D'Amato, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation. [S1] [S3] [S5]
Eight senators cosponsored the bill: 6 Democrats and 2 Republicans. [S4]
On April 30, 1992, the Commerce Committee's Subcommittee on Aviation held a hearing on the bill, printed as S.Hrg. 102-898. [S5]
No further action followed: the full Commerce Committee never reported the bill, no vote was ever held in either chamber, and the bill died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Airlines that might otherwise have faced mandatory hiring and seniority-integration duties when acquiring routes were better off; displaced airline workers gained nothing from the bill's failure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Airlines; displaced airline workers gained nothing

for.name: Sen. Bob Graham
for.role: U.S. Senator from Florida; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and pressed for employee protections in airline route transfers.

for.name: Sen. Al D'Amato
for.role: U.S. Senator from New York; original co-introducer
for.what_they_did: Joined Graham at introduction, making the bill bipartisan from day one.

for.name: Senate Aviation Subcommittee
for.role: Subcommittee of the Senate Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Held a hearing on the bill on April 30, 1992 (S.Hrg. 102-898), the only public consideration it received.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced, held a subcommittee hearing, and never reported it to the full Senate, so no vote ever occurred.

against.name: Sen. Daniel Inouye
against.role: Chairman, Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee that never brought the bill to a markup or floor vote during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Democrat and a Republican together and drew cosponsors from both parties (6 Democrats, 2 Republicans); its death in committee is not attributable to a party-line vote.

industries.note: Airlines acquiring route authority would be required to hire the transferring carrier's employees by seniority and honor their seniority standing, and could face court judgments and legal fees. Hiring airlines would also have to give furloughed workers of any age a first right of hire for 17 years, extending protections that had expired after 10.

industries.industry: Displaced airline employees (pilots, flight attendants, mechanics, ground staff)
industries.note: These workers would gain guaranteed hiring by whoever buys their routes and enforceable seniority protections in federal court. The bill's failure left them with no such rights.
